routes.description: Establish that evaluative and moral concepts arise from factual requirements faced by living, choosing human beings, and that those requirements support objective guidance for flourishing and social conduct.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies life-relevant facts as the referents and standard of evaluation, explains how those facts guide volitional human action, and derives non-arbitrary principles for individual and interpersonal conduct.

motionBridge.description: Connect the factual requirements of human life to truth-apt standards governing choices, actions, and character.

centralBridges.description: Explain why living organisms' conditional requirements create the factual basis and practical need for evaluative concepts.
Show how a human choice to live makes facts about survival and flourishing action-guiding without treating value as an intrinsic property.
Derive rights and constraints on force from human rational agency and each person's need to act on independent judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish emotions accompanying evaluation from the cognitive identification of life-supporting or life-destructive facts.
Apply the life-based standard consistently across immortality, psychopath, animal-treatment, and consent cases.

routes.description: Establish that moral utterances express non-truth-apt emotional attitudes and that factual descriptions of life, agency, or flourishing do not themselves supply objective oughtness or binding interpersonal duties.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it provides a coherent emotivist account of moral language and experience while showing that the proposed life standard cannot non-circularly bridge facts to objective norms or explain its disputed applications.

motionBridge.description: Account for moral claims as emotive expressions while denying that life-related facts constitute objective moral properties or truth conditions.

centralBridges.description: Specify what moral predicates express and require the objectivist alternative to identify the alleged objective oughtness.
Show why a pre-moral choice to live or a factual description of flourishing cannot generate objective normative authority.
Test whether actor-centered life and flourishing can justify rights or condemn advantageous harm without assuming the disputed morality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how emotive advocacy, rational inference, and useful rights conventions can function without objective moral truth.
Use immortality, atypical agents, and animal treatment to test the scope and consistency of the life-based account.

sections.title: Moral Meaning, Emotion, and Objective Reference
sections.rationale: This issue defines the motion-level disagreement over whether moral predicates report life-relevant facts or express attitudes without truth conditions, and it fixes what either side must explain about moral language and cognition.

sections.title: Life, Choice, and the Foundation of Value
sections.rationale: This issue covers the proposed dependence of value on living action and the choice to remain alive, together with the challenge that a conditional or pre-moral choice cannot establish objective value.

sections.title: From Life Facts to Oughts and Flourishing
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central inferential bridge from biological and human facts to action-guiding oughts, including whether flourishing clarifies the standard or expands it beyond survival without an objective warrant.

sections.title: Rational Egoism, Rights, and Moral Agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether a life-centered ethic can derive interpersonal rights and constraints on advantageous harm, and whether psychopath and abnormal-agent cases expose circularity or legitimate limits on moral concepts.

sections.title: Animals, Harm, and Practical Boundaries
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether the competing accounts consistently explain concern for suffering, condemnation of gratuitous harm, differences between human and animal status, and permissibility claims about animal use.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Emotivism treats ethical statements as expressions of non-propositional emotion rather than truth-apt reports about either objective facts or a speaker's preferences.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained opening turn presents the emotivist position associated with Alex O'Connor and contrasts it explicitly with subjectivism.

response.rationale: This is a constructive statement of emotivism, so no earlier opposing move supplies a response demand; it directly establishes the con motion account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the central semantic position and distinguishes it from subjectivism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between non-propositional emotional expression and truth-apt subjectivism is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move defines the speaker's adopted metaethical view rather than making a contingent empirical prediction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The view is explicitly differentiated from subjectivism and its semantic claim is internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is explained specifically, though the broader adequacy of emotivism is not yet defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by specifying the proposed meaning of ethical statements.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is assessed in this introductory statement of the speaker's own position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly contrasts subjectivist truth conditions with emotivism's treatment of ethical statements as emotional expressions.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A materialist moral objectivist must identify what objective oughtness is and explain where it exists or originates if it is not an emotion.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly introduces this as his principal challenge to an objectivist and completes it before yielding the floor.

response.rationale: This constructive challenge specifies the ontological and explanatory burden that the materialist objectivist account must meet; it answers no earlier move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it crisply identifies a central demand, although its spatial framing is somewhat restrictive.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is recoverable, but treating existence as requiring a location leaves 'objective oughtness' partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: An account of oughtness is necessary, but the suggestion that material reality requires simple spatial location overstates the burden.

charity.alternative: Objective oughtness may be a relation, function, or higher-level natural fact rather than a discrete object.
charity.decisiveQualification: A materialist objectivist still owes an account of that relation's normative authority and truth conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core explanatory challenge is sound, but the object-or-location framing leaves a material ontological bridge compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The challenge is conceptually motivated, though no argument establishes that all materialist properties must be spatial objects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the indispensable con semantic and ontological bridge by demanding an account of objective oughtness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The spatial-object framing weakens the strongest naturalist alternative, although the remaining explanatory demand is legitimate.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what good or ought is if not emotion and where it originates under a materialist ontology.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Because only living organisms pursue values to preserve their existence, life is the ultimate factual foundation of value and evaluative concepts.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle develops the life-based derivation continuously, using organisms and their goal-directed activity as the central examples.

response.rationale: This is the foundational pro constructive move, identifying living goal-directed activity as the factual source of evaluative concepts without targeting an earlier objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies the route's factual foundation clearly, while the later normative bridge remains separate.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim concerns the foundation and practical need for value concepts, not an unexplained intrinsic property of life.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim is confined to organisms' conditional requirements and the role of evaluation in continued life.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence of goal pursuit and evaluative need on life is coherent, with one compressed step from examples to universality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Organismic dependence supplies concrete support, but the universal claim about all evaluative concepts receives limited independent defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central factual-basis bridge by explaining why living requirements generate evaluative concepts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own biological foundation and does not materially interpret an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that only living things pursue values and that continued existence requires value-directed activity.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: For volitional human beings, oughts identify life-supporting actions, while chosen values and virtues organize the rational pursuit of continued life and flourishing.
moves.attributionBasis: The same pro turn explicitly moves from the biological basis of value to human choice, rational guidance, moral values, and virtues.

components.text: Explain what objective oughtness is and how it arises within a materialist account rather than from emotion.

response.rationale: The move contacts the demand by construing oughts as rational guidance identifying factual life requirements for volitional agents, though it does not fully explain categorical authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive demand and gives a substantive naturalistic account, but leaves the fact-to-authority bridge underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: Oughts and chosen values are intelligible, but the scope shifts between continued life, flourishing, and moral guidance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The practical need for guidance is supported, but its identification with moral oughtness needs a further normative qualification.

charity.alternative: The con demand concerns normative authority, not merely whether factual information can instrumentally guide chosen goals.
charity.decisiveQualification: Life requirements explain hypothetical guidance but do not by themselves establish an unconditional moral ought.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account coherently links free choice and guidance, but leaves a material bridge from life-supporting means to moral oughts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Facts about volition and survival support instrumental guidance, while the distinct moral warrant remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central normative-guidance bridge by explaining the action-guiding role assigned to oughts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly supplies a naturalistic alternative, while only partially addressing the strongest authority-based version of the challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says humans need rational guidance to live and identifies factual human-life requirements as the moral standard.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Moral objectivity consists in a cognitive relation to life-relevant facts, and evaluative concepts lose their basis when severed from the life conditions that make them necessary.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle directly addresses the outstanding concern about oughtness through Rand's subjective-intrinsic-objective trichotomy and its conceptual consequence.

components.text: Identify the nature and source of objective evaluative truth within a materialist ontology.
Explain why moral evaluation is cognitive and fact-related rather than merely an emotional expression.

response.rationale: The reply locates objectivity in a mind-fact cognitive relation and grounds evaluative concepts in life conditions, contacting both earlier semantic and ontological demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both demands, though defining objectivity does not fully establish the resulting claims' normative authority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mind-fact relation is recoverable, but 'objective' alternates between epistemic relation and moral status without full separation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Life plausibly explains evaluative concepts' need, but the claim that detached evaluation is invalid requires an additional warrant.

charity.alternative: Emotivism can accept cognition about life facts while denying that moral predicates report those facts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing a mind-fact relation does not alone show that moral language has those facts as truth conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed relation is coherent, but the inference from conceptual dependence to objective moral truth remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Life-related facts are identified, although their status as moral truth conditions is asserted more than independently demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by explaining the claimed relation between life facts and objective evaluation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply offers a serious rival account but does not fully engage the strongest semantic distinction available to emotivism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines objective as a connection between mind and fact and says life makes evaluative concepts necessary.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If immortal volitional people could still care about one another and suffer, ethics would remain applicable despite the complete absence of possible death.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly tests Biddle's stated restriction of ethics to mortal life with a developed immortality counterexample.

components.text: Show that life's vulnerability and preservation are necessary for evaluative and ethical concepts.
Show that life-supporting guidance exhausts the practical role of ethical oughts for volitional agents.

response.rationale: The immortal-agent case directly tests whether ethics disappears once death is impossible while suffering and interpersonal concern remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the life-dependence thesis with a focused counterexample, though the hypothetical's conditions remain underspecified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterexample is clear, but immortality may remove death without removing all damage to agency or flourishing.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately offers an imaginable counterexample rather than claiming that immortal persons actually exist.

charity.alternative: The life standard may concern flourishing and functioning rather than merely avoidance of biological death.
charity.decisiveQualification: Immortal agents could still face suffering and impaired functioning, so life-relevant conditions might persist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possibility test is coherent, though it does not fully specify whether immortal agents can suffer irreversible functional harms.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A logically possible counterexample is adequate for testing necessity, subject to the unresolved flourishing qualification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the subsidiary hard-case bridge by testing the scope of the life-based account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The test is fair against a death-centered formulation but does not fully address the stronger flourishing-based interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt imagines people who cannot die yet remain fellow creatures whose treatment appears ethically significant.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A survival-based egoistic ethic appears unable to condemn recreational animal torture when the act neither threatens the torturer's survival nor frustrates that person's preferences.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor introduces the objection as a direct question about rational egoism and develops the animal-torture case through the end of his turn.

components.text: Explain how actor-centered life-supporting guidance condemns conduct that does not harm the actor's survival or preferences.
Show that life's status as value foundation supplies standards regarding another living creature's suffering.

response.rationale: The recreational-torture case directly tests whether the proposed egoistic standard can condemn harm lacking an apparent cost to the agent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly isolates a difficult application and places the missing interpersonal or animal-regarding warrant under direct pressure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The case specifies gratuitous torture, absence of survival cost, and absence of frustrated actor preference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move says the ethic appears unable to condemn the conduct and appropriately invites an account rather than asserting impossibility.

charity.alternative: An egoist may argue that cruelty damages character, practical rationality, or a general life-promoting disposition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hypothetical stipulates no relevant survival or preference cost, requiring an independent connection to those alleged harms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hypothetical cleanly separates intuitive condemnation from the actor's stipulated survival and preference interests.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The counterexample strongly tests the stated standard, with only a bounded gap concerning indirect character effects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the subsidiary hard-case bridge through a concrete animal-treatment application.

representationalCharity.rationale: The counterexample anticipates the central egoistic escape and preserves a focused demand for a non-stipulative warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how rational egoism condemns animal torture when morality is described as whatever supports the actor's survival.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Gratuitous animal abuse is immoral because life supplies a standard of value beyond humans, and purposeless destruction manifests contempt for life.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows O'Connor's animal-abuse question, and the sustained explanation is delivered by Biddle apart from brief acknowledgments.

components.text: Explain why gratuitous animal torture is wrong despite lacking an obvious survival cost to the torturer.

response.rationale: The response condemns unnecessary suffering by extending the life standard beyond humans and characterizing purposeless destruction as anti-life.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive case and states a principle, but does not fully connect contempt for life to the actor's flourishing.

precisionFindings.rationale: The excerpt shifts among pain, flowers, wrongness, and immorality, obscuring the precise scope of the proposed principle.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical condemnation is stronger than the supplied bridge from life as a standard to other-regarding duties.

charity.alternative: The counterexample asks for an egoistic reason binding a torturer whose own life and preferences are unaffected.
charity.decisiveQualification: General respect for life cannot answer that demand unless its contribution to the actor's flourishing is independently shown.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion is compatible with the life standard, but the crucial inference from contempt for life to immorality is unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move rests mainly on asserted opposition to unnecessary pain and an analogy with purposeless flower destruction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the subsidiary hard-case bridge by applying the life standard to gratuitous animal harm.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer addresses the act but weakens the strongest stipulated version by relying on an asserted anti-life disposition.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt opposes unnecessary animal pain and extends life's evaluative role to flowers and dogs, but supplies no further egoistic bridge.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Appealing to contempt for life assumes the disputed value of life and therefore argues circularly against someone who does not already share that valuation.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly labels the preceding justification circular and develops the objection through the flower-kicking example despite brief interruptions.

components.text: Use contempt for life to justify why gratuitous destruction and animal abuse are immoral.
Establish life as the value-conferring foundation without assuming that life is already valuable.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses circularity: contempt for life cannot justify life's value to a person who disputes that valuation, and it states the resulting failure.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the challenged premise, the circular inference, and the consequence for the attempted justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The circularity allegation identifies the disputed premise and confines the objection to using that premise as justification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the diagnosis as how the argument seems and supports it by restating the circular dependence.

charity.alternative: The pro claim may be conceptual: life grounds the possibility of value rather than possessing intrinsic value.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conceptual dependence alone does not establish a reason to respect every life or condemn purposeless destruction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic inference is valid against the stated appeal from contempt for life to life's universal moral importance.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The preceding rationale itself supplies the relevant premise dependence, though the broader foundation thesis may escape circularity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central fact-norm-gap bridge by challenging the non-circular derivation of life's moral authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the strongest conceptual reading while identifying the separate normative conclusion that remains unsupported.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the response argues in a circle because it invokes life's value while that value is being challenged.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Life is not intrinsically valuable; a person's choice to remain alive logically precedes evaluation and creates the need for values and action.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle marks a clarification and gives an extended first-person account of how choosing continued existence grounds the need for valuation.

components.text: Show that the life-based account assumes life's intrinsic value when explaining the origin of evaluation.
Explain how normative guidance arises without positing an intrinsic entity or property called goodness.

response.rationale: The reply denies the premise of intrinsic value and identifies the prior choice to live as what makes valuation practically necessary, defeating that form of circularity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes intrinsic value from the logical precondition of valuing, though objective authority remains unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The logical ordering among choosing life, needing values, and evaluating actions is stated clearly and consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stated conditional framework, rejecting continued life removes the practical need to select life-serving values.

charity.alternative: The circularity objection may target moral authority, not the narrower conceptual possibility of valuation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A pre-moral choice can explain conditional practical reasons without establishing an objective reason to make that choice.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure is coherent and avoids intrinsic value, with the objective status of the initiating choice left open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The practical dependence is illustrated directly, although its generality beyond the first-person choice is not fully established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central normative-guidance bridge by explaining the conditional origin of value and action.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly defeats the intrinsic-value reading but leaves the strongest authority-based version of the objection intact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that only the choice to live makes valuing necessary and that this choice logically precedes evaluation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A pre-moral choice to live cannot supply objective normativity, because an objective requirement to remain alive must be independently established or the resulting moral system remains conditional on a nonobjective choice.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor introduces several objections, then persistently questions whether objectivity can enter through the choice between living and dying.

components.text: Show that a pre-moral choice to live can establish objective rather than merely conditional normative authority.
Establish that life-serving guidance binds agents beyond their antecedent nonobjective commitment to living.

response.rationale: The move expressly identifies the conditionality problem and states that independent objective support for remaining alive is required to obtain objective morality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly targets the decisive premise and clearly states the consequence if the initiating choice lacks objective authority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among pre-moral choice, conditional reasons, and objective reasons is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: For an objective conclusion, the objection correctly requires either objective support for the choice or another binding bridge.

charity.alternative: The pro account may seek objective hypothetical imperatives conditional on choosing life, not a categorical duty to live.
charity.decisiveQualification: That interpretation preserves factual guidance but narrows the claimed objective morality to agents sharing the condition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dilemma between independently justified life choice and merely conditional morality is explicit and strongly valid.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant follows from the pro account's express classification of the choice as preceding moral evaluation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central fact-norm-gap bridge by exposing the conditionality of the proposed oughts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accurately grants the conditional account and isolates the remaining categorical or motion-level limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether remaining alive is objectively right after the pro speaker calls that choice pre-moral and pre-rational.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: The requirements of human life support universal moral principles, including individual rights, because each person's life is their own and requires action on personal judgment.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle answers directly with the Frederick Douglass slavery example and develops the classification-based principle culminating in individual rights.

components.text: Explain how a life-based standard generates objective principles extending beyond an individual's conditional choice.
Explain how an actor-centered ethic can recognize constraints concerning other living beings.

response.rationale: The move offers universal human nature and personal ownership of life as a route to rights, contacting interpersonal extension but not resolving the prior-choice authority gap or animal case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary interpersonal consequence but leaves the decisive pre-moral-choice demand substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed progression from human nature to self-ownership and rights is clear, though the ownership premise remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Universal human requirements support general principles, but the asserted derivation of rights needs an additional interpersonal warrant.

charity.alternative: The con objection permits universal facts while denying that they generate binding duties from a pre-moral choice.
charity.decisiveQualification: Saying each life belongs to its person asserts a normative premise not derived from those universal facts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account identifies relevant facts, but the inference from separate lives to ownership and enforceable rights remains substantial.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human nature and independent lives are asserted as support, with little defense of the self-ownership bridge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rights-and-social-principles bridge by proposing a derivation of individual rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the interpersonal concern but does not fully preserve the strongest fact-norm formulation of the objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt moves from universal human nature and each person's separate life to morality and individual rights.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A murderer who values his own life and genuinely benefits from killing an innocent person is a counterexample to grounding moral obligation solely in the actor's life and flourishing.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly separates the actor from the victim and constructs the hypothetical through repeated clarification after Biddle questions its realism.

components.text: Show why another person's rights bind an actor when violating them genuinely advances the actor's own flourishing.
Show that choosing one's own life generates constraints protecting another person's life.

response.rationale: The stipulated beneficial murder directly tests whether actor-centered flourishing yields an exceptionless prohibition protecting an innocent person's separate life.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly isolates the actor-beneficiary issue and removes ordinary prudential costs to test the proposed rights derivation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothetical clearly stipulates innocence, genuine benefit, the actor's commitment to life, and interpersonal separation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A stipulated possible counterexample is proportionate to challenging an allegedly universal derivation of rights.

charity.alternative: The pro account may deny that murder can genuinely promote long-term rational flourishing because force undermines human social conditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hypothetical stipulates genuine all-things-considered benefit, so a universal principle must address that possibility rather than ordinary consequences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample validly pressures any universal prohibition derived solely from the actor's own all-things-considered flourishing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hypothetical needs no empirical frequency showing, though its metaphysical possibility under richer flourishing remains contestable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central interpersonal-counterexamples bridge by testing rights against advantageous harm.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly anticipates empirical-prudential replies and preserves the decisive normative question under the stipulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stipulates an innocent victim and a murderer whose own life and flourishing genuinely improve through killing.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Invoking rights to constrain rational egoism presupposes the objective moral properties under dispute and does not explain why an egoist should care about another person's rights.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor directly identifies rights as the allegedly assumed premise and follows Biddle's brief denials with a focused question about their egoistic basis.

components.text: Derive individual rights from life requirements rather than assuming the disputed moral status of other persons.
Explain why an egoist's choice of personal life creates reasons to respect another person's rights.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses rights as an assumed normative premise and states that invoking them does not explain their authority for the egoist.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the alleged presupposition and states the defeating consequence for the rights-based answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection distinguishes possessing rights from explaining why those rights bind an egoistic actor.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The charge is proportionate because the preceding derivation introduced ownership and rights without a defended normative bridge.

charity.alternative: Rights may summarize factual conditions of mutually beneficial freedom rather than primitive moral properties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must still explain why an advantaged violator is bound when mutual benefit or prudential cost is stipulated away.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference correctly distinguishes naming a constraint from deriving its binding force within rational egoism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The preceding appeal to personal ownership and rights supplies specific support for the presupposition diagnosis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central interpersonal-counterexamples bridge by challenging the derivation and authority of rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection grants a naturalistic functional account while isolating its unresolved authority over exceptional egoists.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what rights are and why a rational egoist concerned with personal survival should care about another's rights.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Individual rights recognize the factual human need for freedom to act on rational judgment, while rights violators may forfeit freedom needed to threaten others.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly gives Biddle the floor to define rights, and the sustained answer presents his stated Objectivist position.

components.text: Explain what rights are and why their constraints arise from human life rather than being presupposed moral properties.
Explain why force remains impermissible when a particular violator might personally benefit from it.

response.rationale: The response defines rights functionally through humans' need for freedom from force, contacting the presupposition demand but not the stipulated advantageous-violator case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers what rights recognize and their general purpose, while leaving one decisive exceptional-agent component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Rights, freedom from force, independent agency, and forfeiture by violators are stated with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Freedom is strongly connected to rational agency, but universal enforceable rights require more than a general functional need.

charity.alternative: The con objection challenges binding authority in exceptional cases, not the general usefulness of noncoercive institutions.
charity.decisiveQualification: A social function does not alone show why every advantaged violator has a moral duty to comply.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The functional account coherently explains rights' general purpose, with a material gap from need to universal constraint.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human dependence on independent judgment supports freedom, but the enforcement and forfeiture conclusions are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rights bridge by defining rights through factual requirements of rational freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response offers a substantive naturalistic account but only partly handles the strongest exception-focused challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines a right as recognition that humans need freedom from force to live as independent agents.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Emotions register a person's values but are not instruments of knowledge; rational inquiry identifies life as the objective standard of moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: The first answer to the audience question expressly identifies Objectivism and develops its account of emotion, reason, and the standard of life.

components.text: Explain why emotional expression does not exhaust moral cognition or determine moral truth.
Identify a non-emotional route for knowing good, bad, right, and wrong.

response.rationale: The response distinguishes emotions as registrations of prior values from rational cognition and identifies life as the proposed rational standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the epistemic contrast, though it does not fully answer emotivism's semantic rather than epistemic thesis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinct roles assigned to emotion, reason, moral knowledge, and life's standard are plainly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The emotion-reason distinction is clear, but life's status as the objective standard is asserted with limited added warrant.

charity.alternative: Emotivism is a semantic account of ethical utterances and need not claim emotions are instruments of factual knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that reason discovers life facts does not by itself refute the claim that moral utterances express attitudes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemic distinction is coherent, but its use against emotivism leaves a material semantic bridge unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account of emotions is asserted plausibly, while the conclusion that life is the moral standard is reiterated rather than defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary emotion-and-cognition bridge by separating affect from rational identification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply partially conflates emotivism with an epistemic reliance on feeling and misses the strongest semantic formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says emotions reflect values but are not means of knowledge, while reason identifies life as the standard.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Emotivism explains differential concern for animals through emotional resemblance and attachment more naturally than a rational-egoist derivation does.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly introduces the point as his response and contrasts an emotivist framework with Objectivism using developed examples.

components.text: Show whether emotional mechanisms can explain stable moral concern without functioning as instruments of factual knowledge.
Explain differential moral concern for animals without deriving it from a universal life standard.
Explain practical moral boundaries without objective rights or rational-egoist derivation.

response.rationale: The response offers resemblance and attachment as an emotive explanation of animal boundaries, contacting two issues but not the distinct rights-function demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a substantive partial answer about animal concern, while its selected incest example weakly represents the broader proposition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but the excerpt shifts from animals to incest and from explanation to comparative adequacy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents emotivism as seeming to explain boundaries and acknowledges the examples' uncomfortable character.

charity.alternative: A rational account may treat emotional resemblance as causal psychology while still evaluating resulting attitudes by life-relevant reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: Emotivism's psychological naturalness does not establish that rational evaluation adds no explanatory or normative work.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Emotional resemblance can coherently explain differential concern, though explanatory naturalness does not prove semantic truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on illustrative animal and taboo examples without representative evidence or serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con subsidiary boundary-case bridge through an emotive account of differential concern.

representationalCharity.rationale: The comparison recognizes rational alternatives but characterizes some efforts as hoop-jumping without fully testing their strongest form.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims emotivism makes sense of graded concern and illustrates emotionally grounded boundaries with a widespread taboo.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Human life as the standard of value means flourishing through the full exercise of human capacities, not mere biological survival, and is more fundamental than happiness.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is directed to Craig and invokes Rand; the answer expressly states Rand's position and Biddle's agreement with it.

components.text: Test the life standard as a standard of flourishing and full human functioning rather than mere avoidance of death.
Clarify what 'life' denotes in the value standard before assessing whether its use is circular.
Explain why flourishing supplies objective authority rather than merely elaborating a chosen end.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing mere biological survival with survival qua human capacities and flourishing, preserving the scope question while not resolving authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe is explicit and relevant to earlier survival objections, but it leaves the central conditionality challenge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly rejects mere survival, though flourishing and full capacities are not operationally specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The semantic clarification is supported as the adopted view, but equivalence among life, flourishing, and happiness is compressed.

charity.alternative: Earlier objections targeted biological survival because the account repeatedly appealed to continued existence and life preservation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Broadening life to flourishing is legitimate only if the broader standard receives an independent and non-circular specification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The clarification is internally consistent, but the move from biological life to full-capacity flourishing needs further specification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move states and attributes the broader interpretation, with limited defense for why it is the fundamental standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central normative-guidance bridge by specifying the human-life end that oughts guide.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly corrects a narrow reading while leaving the strongest concern about the enlarged standard's warrant visible.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says human life does not mean mere survival but survival qua human capacities, essentially flourishing.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Human life or flourishing does not adequately define moral goodness because it omits familiar ethical concern for other people and animals.
moves.attributionBasis: The question asks Alex what evidence would persuade him, and his sustained answer identifies definitional and existential requirements before applying them to rational egoism.

components.text: Show that human flourishing adequately captures the content ordinarily expressed by moral goodness.
Explain how actor-centered human life captures familiar concern for other people.
Explain how the proposed standard captures familiar moral concern for animals.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges flourishing's semantic adequacy and identifies concern for other humans and animals as omitted components.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the broadened definition and supplies two concrete domains that allegedly exceed its content.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes understanding the proposed referent from accepting it as an adequate definition of morality.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is presented as the speaker's considered semantic judgment rather than as a demonstrated universal linguistic fact.

charity.alternative: Human flourishing may include social relationships, benevolence, and principled treatment of animals rather than narrow self-preservation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must derive those inclusions rather than importing familiar moral concern into an otherwise actor-centered standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The semantic objection coherently separates a proposed natural referent from the broader content moral discourse appears to carry.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: People and animals are concrete counterdomains, though claims about ordinary moral meaning lack representative linguistic evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central semantic account by testing whether flourishing supplies adequate moral truth conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection allows the broader flourishing proposal while identifying the non-circular derivation it still owes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts the proposed terms but denies that human life or flourishing captures what people mean by morality.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: General biological values differ from moral values, which arise within the sphere of human choice; valuing animal life therefore does not entail granting animals human rights.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig directly answers the audience member's follow-up and continues the same account of values, morality, rights, and animals.

components.text: Explain how the account distinguishes concern for animal life from specifically human moral status and rights.
Provide a rational rather than purely emotive account of differing moral treatment across species.
Explain why animals can matter without possessing human rights.

response.rationale: The response distinguishes general biological values from choice-dependent moral values and uses that distinction to explain concern without animal rights.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the boundary issue and clarifies status, though it does not fully justify the denial of all animal rights.

precisionFindings.rationale: Biological value, moral value, human choice, and rights are expressly distinguished with stable domains.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Choice plausibly differentiates moral agency, but it does not by itself entail that animals possess no rights or protections.

charity.alternative: Animals could lack moral agency yet retain rights or claims grounded in sentience, interests, or vulnerability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinguishing chosen moral values from biological values does not independently exclude patient-based rights.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The agency distinction is coherent, but the inference from nonagency to absence of rights contains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human choice supports a difference in moral agency, while the categorical rights conclusion is largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the subsidiary hard-case bridge by clarifying biological, moral, human, and animal domains.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes agency but omits the strongest alternative basis for animal moral status.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes general biological value from choice-dependent human morality and concludes that animals do not have rights.
